note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi made a wedding for his son, Rabbi Shimon. On the wedding canopy was written that 24,000 myriad dinars had been spent on it, yet he did not invite bar Kappara. Bar Kappara said: if those who go against God's will get such reward, how much more those who do His will. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi then invited him, and bar Kappara said: if those who do His will get this much in this world, how much more in the World-to-Come. In another episode, because calamity struck the world on any day Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi laughed, he offered bar Kappara forty se'a of wheat not to make him laugh. Bar Kappara put a tar-smeared basket upside down on his head and came to collect his wheat; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi laughed, and bar Kappara said he was only taking what he was owed.
why: The discussion has moved from kinds of figs to a story of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi marveling at a thousand fig dishes; it continues with stories of his wealth and his dealings with bar Kappara.

note: Isi bar Yehuda stayed away from Rabbi Yosei's academy for three days. Vardimus, Rabbi Yosei's son, found him and asked why. Isi said he could not attend when he did not understand Rabbi Yosei's reasoning, and named the puzzle: Rabbi Yosei teaches that a town's own laundry takes precedence over the lives of others, but what verse is that based on? Vardimus explained it from the verse about the land around the Levite cities, which is for their animals and for all their beasts. The word for beasts can also be read as their lives, and since that would be obvious, it must mean something vital to life, namely laundry, because grimy clothes cause real suffering.
why: The Gemara returns to Rabbi Yosei's ruling that a town's laundry comes before others' lives, and the story supplies the verse behind it before the discussion turns to Rabbi Yosei's view of vows about bathing.
